2123172397897621508.text:
Anthropic doesn't see itself as a "normal company." Dario Amodei believes both that 1) superintelligent AI could destroy humanity, and 2) our only chance at survival is to have his trillion-dollar tech company build it first.

This is not an intuitive way to think about either capitalism or social change, but it’s led Anthropic to the eve of one of the biggest IPOs in history. So it's more important than ever for the public to understand and scrutinize its idiosyncratic theory of change.

A handful of observations on the popular politics of AI:

1) Americans fear and dislike AI (even those who use it!) and a majority are now worried about extinction too. >80% would rather slow down than “beat China.”

2) But they’re not yet willing to vote on the issue. Trump’s accelerationism is a bet that voters care about the stock market way more than they care about AI. This trade-off is probably (politically) correct for now.

3) We’re already seeing a partisan divide emerge as a result. One failure mode for AI policy is if it ends up like climate or Covid: an ostensibly scientific issue that gets irreversibly polarized.

4) I could see a pause becoming a Dem litmus test in the 2028 primaries, and "pacing" wil be the watered-down moderate solution. It'll be tough to justify on a televised debate stage why we should let development continue at all.

5) But this all explodes once we get a bigger warning shot. Bipartisan action is easier on concrete, direct harms (e.g. data centers, kids’ safety). If the next AI incident takes down a hospital or electricity grid, no voter will tolerate laissez-faire.

6) Plus, all incentives point to raising salience: elites disproportionately care about AI, and politicians will keep talking through the midterms and primaries. Also, more incidents!

7) Public opinion is still quite malleable, and most politicians are still figuring out what they think. Lots of degrees of freedom here — there's hope in the fact that this policy arena is refreshingly non-predetermined!

More in the blog post: https://t.co/cs8jCOfpOH

It's pub day for The AGI Chronicles!

Impossible to convey how hard this thing was to write. I locked myself away for a year, and interviewed more than 150 AI insiders to try to get the full story of the race between OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind, because it felt so important to have an accurate record of how we got here.

But it's done, and it's out, and you can start reading it today! (Or listening -- I recorded the audiobook myself.) I'm very happy with the finished product, and I hope it will serve as both a durable artifact of this era and a sense-making instrument for people who are getting up to speed on AI.

I'm not very good at street-team promo, but if you buy a copy and reply with your receipt, I will generate a beautiful personalized thank-you poem as a token of my gratitude.

quoted.author: NYMag
quoted.text:
On September 8, Jacob Coxon, a 27-year-old Anthropic employee, posted a resignation statement on X that ricocheted around the internet. He quit in protest of what he saw as the company’s suicidally reckless pursuit of artificial general intelligence. To the AI community, an Anthropic employee believing that the technology their company is developing might end the world is not exactly news. (Anthropic was founded by former OpenAI employees who believed OpenAI, if left unchecked, would do just that.) But an Anthropic employee publicly quitting in protest is.

Afterward, a debate broke out: If you’re a lab employee who believes in these risks, what should you do? Is it best to leave in protest? Or is it better to agitate from the inside, close to the seat of power? And how would the choice affect your friendships and community?

“For me, there’s quite a distinction between my rational beliefs and the things I feel in my gut,” says Coxon. “If you’d asked me to narrate my opinions when entering Anthropic and when leaving Anthropic, they would probably sound pretty similar. But in terms of the actual feeling between the start and the end, it just felt very, very different.”

Coxon joins a small set of employees of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind who, over the years, chose to walk away.

For our Cover Story, in collaboration with Asterisk Magazine, we brought together eight of them. They don’t share the same concerns or the same p(dooms) — in fact, they wouldn’t necessarily agree that p(doom) is a coherent concept. But together, they provide a candid view of the AI race and the individual calculus many employees face.

Read their interviews in full: https://t.co/u5wik8vlXM
